key_insight: Among Medicaid-enrolled preschoolers with untreated cavities, more than half still had a dental treatment gap within one year, even after visiting a dentist.
clinical_relevance: This suggests pediatric primary care may be a useful place to help prevent progression of early childhood caries when dental treatment is delayed or incomplete.
method: Retrospective cohort study using data from 18 community pediatric primary care practices in Northeastern Ohio (2017-2022)
Followed Medicaid claims to see whether children received dental treatment within 1 year of enrollment
Used multivariable logistic regression to test factors linked to treatment gaps
evidence_signal: Of 766 eligible children, 487 attended a dentist within one year; among the 155 with baseline untreated decay, 90 (58.1%) had fewer treated teeth than decayed teeth at baseline.
watch_item: A treatment gap may reflect access barriers or dentists' reluctance to restore primary teeth, so implementation of preventive alternatives still needs careful coordination and follow-up.
paper_title: Treatment Gaps Among Young Medicaid-Enrolled Children with Tooth Decay in Pediatric Primary Care
